newsitem.title: GERMANY: Genscher warns Bonn over delays in Czech agreement.
newsitem.headline: Genscher warns Bonn over delays in Czech agreement.

text.p: Germany's former foreign minister Hans-Dietrich Genscher warned on Wednesday any more delays in completing a reconciliation pact between Germany and the Czech Republic could damage Bonn's international reputation.
Genscher, writing in Berlin's Tagesspiegel newspaper, said Germany's failure to complete the treaty after years of talks had now stirred opponents of the reconciliation in Prague.
"Any further delay would have negative consequences -- not only for German-Czech relations," Genscher said. "We should all be aware of that and what is at stake here."
Genscher, who was foreign minister from 1974 to 1992, said the credibility and reliability of Germany and its foreign policies could be tarnished by failure to complete the treaty.
"What had to happen has now happened -- the years of back and forth over the German-Czech declaration has now awoken opposing forces in Prague," Genscher said.
Czech Foreign Minister Josef Zieleniec said recently the treaty was ready for signing as far as Prague was concerned.
The text to resolve the last major World War Two dispute between Germany and one of its neighbours only needed approval from Bonn, Zieleniec said in a newspaper interview this month.
The agreement is expected to regulate issues of property and compensation for both Czech victims of Nazi aggression and for millions of ethnic Germans driven out of Czechoslovakia.
Chancellor Helmut Kohl said last month he hoped the declaration could be signed this year.

But Kohl's coalition allies, the Bavarian Christian Social Union (CSU), have consistently championed the cause of the 2.5 million ethnic "Sudeten Germans" forced to leave after the war and demanded Prague negotiate directly with expellees' groups.
"The Germans are primarily to blame for the delays," said Antje Vollmer, a vice president of the German parliament and member of the opposition Greens party.
The Czech parliament's chairman, Milos Zeman, has indicated the main problem may be how to describe the Sudetens' removal.

Prague wants the word "transfer" which is used in the 1945 Potsdam agreement when the victorious World War Two allies authorised the former Czechoslovakia to throw out the Sudetens. Bonn is believed to want a stronger word such as expulsion.
"This whole thing could have been finished a year ago. But the chancellor has now given his word it will be finished by the end of the year," Vollmer told German radio.
"That is very important...The biggest disaster that could now happen would be failure to complete the treaty."

Criticism has mounted in Germany over failure to agree the text after more than a year of tortuous negotiations intended to close the book on the Nazi occupation of Czechoslovakia and the subsequent expulsion of millions of ethnic Germans.
Many Czechs see the CSU, the Bavarian sister party of Kohl's Christian Democrats, as the chief obstacle to an agreement.
Over a million Sudeten Germans or their descendants live in Bavaria and the CSU, a member of the ruling coalition in Bonn, has made their cause its own.
